item.title: To Rekindle a Relationship, Managing Memory Is Crucial
item.description:
Memory

To Rekindle a Relationship, Managing Memory Is Crucial

How to work with our memories and act on them when restarting a relationship.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Before we reunite with an ex, what broke us up still remains and what brought us together also still remains.
  • Renewing a relationship can work, depending on our motivations, our memories, and a commitment to change.
  • By drawing on the potential of memory to support us, we can nourish a rekindled relationship.
  • Collective memories define a relationship, reminding us what we mean to each other.

It’s not uncommon for people to split up and then get back together again, at least for a while. But before taking action and reuniting, former couples need to ask themselves why they want to get back together.

Source: Gary Barnes/Pexels

Sometimes, we rekindle a former relationship primarily because of sex deprivation.1 Other times, the primary motivation is acute loneliness or a strong longing just to see the other person. Still other times, we may feel that what defined us before the breakup is suddenly gone and our identity is uncertain.

But none of these motivations will sustain a renewed relationship. In fact, a sense of lost identity may lead to personal instability if the relationship starts again.

This post focuses on renewed romantic relationships motivated by a genuine desire to rekindle the relationship and keep the flame going.

With this genuine desire, we must first acknowledge that rekindling is not the same as beginning a new relationship. And the main difference is that each person has memories of what happened the first time—divisive memories as well as bonding memories.

One key to deciding about reuniting and making things work the second time is how we manage and interpret these memories of the first time. Another key is acting on the memories with real change in ourselves and in the relationship.

Managing Shared Memory When Rekindling a Romance

Balanced Recall. Memory can idealize and memory can vilify. If we are missing someone, memory will select idealized positive images. If we are feeling angry, memory will select images that support this anger.

But we do not want to selectively remember only the good times or only the struggles. To achieve a representative sampling of memory, we need to welcome favorable memories as well as unpleasant memories, the highlights and the lowlights. And that takes effort.

To balance recall, choose one consequential event that reminds you why the romantic relationship ended. Put yourself back in that place and time by focusing on specific images or feelings. Then let that memory lead to related memories. Next, do the same with a consequential event that felt supportive and loving. Continue this memory exercise with different consequential memories until you feel a sense of comprehensiveness.

There's no objective or logical conclusion to the exercise, but after engaging in balanced recall, memory for the relationship will be more representative, and emotional impressions will be more clear.

Source: Nam Phong Bui/Pexels

The Experiencing Self and the Remembering Self. We have an experiencing self that feels events in the present and a remembering self that looks back and considers the memories of these events. Notably, we experience events consistently and fully throughout, but we remember events primarily in terms of how they end.2

If we take a delightful one-week vacation, but the last full day is especially frustrating and unpleasant, our memory will deemphasize the delightful first six days and highlight the aversive ending, letting it cast its image over the entire vacation. But the end of the story is not the story.

To evaluate the potential for reuniting with an ex, we need to consider the former relationship as a whole, which means accessing not only our remembering self, with its focus on endings, but our experiencing self as well. This starts by sampling and recalling specific events throughout the relationship.

I am not suggesting that we diminish or deny the breakup itself. Rather, I am recommending more thorough and accurate memory of the trajectory of the relationship. Relationships are full of middles. Recalling and highlighting the events in the middle will allow us to appreciate the entire arc of experiences, addressing significant unpleasantness and significant joys, and some of the times in between.

Using Memories to Make Meaningful Changes

Deep romantic feelings are wonderful, but they are not sufficient for rekindling a relationship. It is necessary to commit to resolving the problems that brought about the breakup.

Each couple needs to clarify what led to their breakup and discuss the changes that will keep those reasons from cropping up again. Proactivity is called for—not optimism or pessimism. We should remember the breakup collaboratively and honestly.

We also need to trust our former selves. There were reasons we broke up, which means reuniting will not work without a commitment to making changes. And the changes should be focused.

If the breakup came about from financial difficulties, new finances must be mapped out, possibly with more dedicated income and a comfortably tighter budget. With substance abuse, the abuse must end—with a commitment to sobriety and consideration of a tailored therapeutic program. If there’s a consensus that too much time with work led to a breakdown of togetherness and intimacy, then clear, tangible reductions in work need to be specified. If it’s agreed that one person was too preoccupied with work, then their devotion to work must be moderated—possibly along with an adjustment of expectations by the other person.

Source: Viktoria Slowikowska

Moving Ahead: Using Memory to Nurture a Renewed Relationship

Forming New Collective Memories. Just as personal episodic memories define individual selves, shared memories define a relationship, reminding us what we mean to each other. Adding new mutual memories will strengthen a rekindled relationship and encourage it to grow.

Memory is connected to and distinguished by place, so going different places together will form new vivid memories that endure. Travel especially encourages new memories, and it need not be extensive. Day trips, visits to unfamiliar neighborhoods in one’s town, or a break in geographic routine can provide distinctive place cues for new shared memories.

Collaborative Remembering. Noteworthy long-term memories experienced by both partners are referred to as relationship-defining memories. An extensive meta-analysis of couples showed that agreement on these relationship-defining memories is positively related to measures of relationship quality and negatively related to splitting up.

The same applies to relationship re-defining memories.

Recalling Good Times and Laughter. A substantial study of married couples showed that thinking about vivid, positive, and emotional memories significantly correlates with higher marital satisfaction. In particular, recalling events when we laughed hard with our partner increases relationship satisfaction more than any other type of happy event.

This elevated relationship satisfaction connects directly to the research on laughter itself, which creates considerable physical and emotional benefits. By recalling a time of uncontrollable laughter with our partner, we bring back a primary memory of that uninhibited time, retrieving, and reliving the sights, sounds, and joyful emotions.

Preparing for Conflict. When my family-therapist spouse was once asked the secret to our long marriage, her answer was neither romantic nor cliché. She said our secret was that we were very good at conflict resolution.

Source: Pavel Danilyuk/Pexels

The same goes for rekindled relationships. Reunited couples will enjoy their renewed intimacy, but they will also experience conflict. When new conflicts arise, couples need to be open to addressing and resolving them.

Closing Words

Of the people who divorce and then remarry each other, 70 percent stay remarried, which is more than twice the percentage for second marriages in general. Renewing relationships can work, depending on the motivations, the memories, and the commitment and effort to change. It's difficult for all of these factors to come together successfully, but not impossible.

One guiding theme is this: When we begin rekindling a relationship, what broke us up still remains, but what brought us together also still remains.

item.title: Gym Body, Pilates Princess, or Yoga Bod?
item.description:
Body Image

Gym Body, Pilates Princess, or Yoga Bod?

Are there now more diverse feminine body ideals to choose from?

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • The visibly muscular, lean gym body continues to appears in social media sites.
  • The thin and softly toned Pilates princess is a new trend in social media, particularly for younger women.
  • The lean and flexible yoga bod remains highly visible in social media.
  • All three ideals are unrealistic for most women, and more diverse representations of fit bodies are needed.
Source: Institutio Alpha Fitness/Pexels

Social media now acts as a platform to effectively circulate different images of idealized bodies and to popularize them into fitness trends. The current trends include the gym body, the Pilates princess, and the yoga bod.

The Gym Body

In her recent research, Bridgette Desjardins (2026) observed that social media has depicted “the image of muscular, spandex-covered fitfluencers” (p. 203) during the last decade. This ideal is sometimes dubbed the gym body: the lean, muscular body shaped through a consistent weight training regimen. This coincides with the rise of CrossFit and with an associated phrase, “strong is the new sexy.”

Despite the acceptance of more muscular feminine bodies, Desjardins emphasized that women with more muscular looks tend to opt for a conventional feminine appearance outside of the gym. Regardless, Desjardins considered that more women are now encouraged to participate in strength sports such as powerlifting to build visible muscle definition.

The Pilates Princess

While the images of the gym body continue to circulate, another quite different image has recently been popularized, particularly via TikTok. The Pilates princess, characterized in the popular media as a slim, slightly toned, and youthful body ideal, is sometimes hailed as the opposite of a gym body. In the popular imagination, this body is to be built specifically on Pilates equipment called the reformer.

Source: Nicholas Fu / Pexels

As a recent trend, there is no research on the actual social media representation, but a Pilates princess appears to embrace an entire lifestyle of regular Pilates reformer classes in tight-fitting (often pink) workout attire, with an emphasis on effortlessly building—as opposed to hard workouts by the gym body—a feminine body through a soft, mindful, healthy lifestyle.

The Yoga Bod

The Pilates princess image has no doubt increased the popularity of reformer Pilates classes. But as a body built with a specific lifestyle, it seems similar to the yoga bod that has appeared in popular media already for several decades.

Source: Victorya Sergeeva/Pexels

Previous research has identified women’s yoga body image as white, thin, and young with exposed skin (particularly in the upper body). While Angela Hinz and colleagues (2021) found that this image of the yoga body also dominates social media representations, Alysse Bailey and colleagues (2022) added that even such sites as #YogaForEveryone that intend to draw a wider variety of practitioners to yoga continue to offer programs to build a thin and toned body. Similar to the Pilates princess, the yoga bod, they continue, is promised to be easily achieved yet requires disciplined practice.

Unlike the Pilates princess, the yoga bod is characteristically flexible. Hinz and colleagues reported that depictions of advanced balance poses dominate social media. Bailey and colleagues added that flexibility—exemplified by displays of splits and backbends—appears to be the main goal of yoga practice in the sites they analyzed.

Although this hyperflexibility requires advanced practice, the posts also created the illusion that it was achievable for beginners. While the posts in Bailey and colleagues’ study emphasized proper alignment, Hinz and colleagues found that advanced poses were sometimes performed with potentially unsafe alignment.

Are These Realistic Body Standards?

There is no evidence that any of these ideals dominate the social media sphere, and women now seem to have more choice in building their exercising bodies, whether it is the slightly toned Pilates princess, lean, flexible muscularity of the yoga bod, or visible muscle definition of the gym body.

However, the researchers still caution that these images all represent ideals that are difficult, if not impossible, to achieve for most women. All are thin bodies that, regardless of the level of muscularity, require significant work to shape and maintain. In addition, social media sites can promote weight training, yoga, and Pilates as fast weight-loss methods, yet these exercise forms, in the absence of a cardiovascular element, are not effective as such. In addition to the promise of improving appearance, maintaining the Pilates princess body or the yoga bod also requires a specific lifestyle with a level of consumerism that adds to their exclusiveness.

These images, the researchers remind us, do not fully reflect the original intent of yoga as advancing holistic mindful practice of well-being, Pilates as a method for functional everyday movement ability, weight training as increasing muscle strength and/or endurance, or the lived, embodied experiences of their practitioners. However, they can have a significant impact on how we women feel about our bodies and then prevent us from creating and maintaining a positive body image. We need to continue to critically assess the media images and find sites, studios, or gyms with solid expert knowledge to choose an exercise form, not based on false promises of quick weight loss, but based on what we enjoy about being physically active.

item.title: Why Do Some People Remember Nearly Every Day of Their Lives?
item.description:
Memory

Why Do Some People Remember Nearly Every Day of Their Lives?

Two new HSAM cases point to memories that frequently return on their own.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Two case reports offer a new clue to the 20-year mystery of highly superior autobiographical memory (HSAM).
  • Standard memory tests have not explained this extraordinary autobiographical recall.
  • Two new cases link HSAM with unusually frequent involuntary autobiographical memories.
  • These involuntary memories may strengthen memory for past experiences through repeated mental rehearsal.

Without looking it up, what can you remember from November 5, 2021? Anything? Me neither. Most of us might remember a major holiday or personal milestone, but little more. A person with highly superior autobiographical memory, or HSAM, may rapidly tell you what day of the week it was, what happened in their life, and what was unfolding in the news.

HSAM is a rare memory ability whereby a person can remember nearly all of their life experiences from adolescence onward. This unusual ability has perplexed researchers for two decades. It has now been 20 years since Elizabeth Parker, Larry Cahill and James McGaugh identified the first known case. Although additional cases have continued to emerge over the years, researchers have struggled to determine what distinguishes people with HSAM from everyone else. People with HSAM often perform unremarkably on standard neuropsychological assessments and common laboratory memory tasks. They are also vulnerable to false memory formation and don’t appear to have a general-purpose memory advantage.

Have Researchers Been Looking in the Wrong Place?

Two newly published case reports offer an important clue about what may distinguish people with HSAM.

In the first, my colleagues and I report on a case of a 16-year-old who we confirmed to have HSAM. When we gave her a date, she immediately named the day of the week and began recalling the events of that day. She could describe whether it was a school day, whether she had taken a test, what she and others had worn, what she ate, and what was happening in her region. As in previous case reports of people with HSAM, she did not stand out on standard neuropsychological assessments or laboratory tasks.

However, we decided to examine something that researchers had not looked at before: her involuntary autobiographical memory.

Most research on human memory, including previous research on HSAM, focuses on voluntary retrieval, when we deliberately try to recall a fact, piece of knowledge, or past experience. Yet, previous HSAM case reports have included anecdotal descriptions suggesting that their participant’s exceptional remembering is not deliberate. Instead, it seems to happen automatically.

This led us to wonder whether people with HSAM differ not in voluntary memory but in involuntary autobiographical memory, when personal memories just seemingly spontaneously pop into our mind (like if, while writing a work email, a past vacation moment suddenly pops into mind). Having these is a normal part of human experience, but we wondered whether someone with HSAM might experience them more often than the average person.

So, we administered a questionnaire called the Involuntary Autobiographical Memory Inventory (IAMI) to the person we identified as having HSAM. In our newly published case report, we show that this person scored two standard deviations above the sample mean reported in prior research, indicating an unusually high frequency of involuntary autobiographical memories. We hypothesize that when past experiences repeatedly enter awareness, they may receive a kind of unplanned mental rehearsal, strengthening those memories over time. This repeated, unplanned rehearsal may support memory consolidation, the process through which memories become more stable over time.

Soon after our report appeared, a European research group led by Krystian Barzykowski published a case study of another 16-year-old with HSAM. They used both the IAMI questionnaire and a newly developed laboratory task designed to capture involuntary autobiographical memories as they occurred. During the task, the participant monitored a monotonous set of patterns on a screen and was periodically asked what had been going through his mind, such as daydreams or involuntary autobiographical memories. On both measures, the participant showed a higher-than-average frequency of involuntary remembering.

Together, these two newly published case reports provide an important new clue about what might underlie HSAM.

For 20 years, researchers largely studied whether people with HSAM are better at deliberately retrieving memories. These two cases suggest a different possibility: Perhaps the crucial difference lies in how often memories return on their own. Of course, two cases cannot tell us whether this pattern characterizes everyone with HSAM, or whether frequent involuntary remembering is a cause of the ability, a result of it, or merely associated with it. But the convergence points to a promising question for future research. If that pattern appears in more people with HSAM, the mystery may turn out to be less about an extraordinary ability to search memory for the past and more about a past that repeatedly returns on its own.

item.title: Do We Fall for People Like Us?
item.description:
Personality

Do We Fall for People Like Us?

We are drawn to people like us, but perhaps not for the reasons we think.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • We tend to look for people who are similar to us in certain ways.
  • Long-term couples are often similar in their moral values, education, and interests.
  • Personality similarity may matter less to relationship duration and quality than we think.

As a personality psychologist, I am occasionally approached for advice on how to build a new app or platform for bringing people together.

Once, it was students who wanted to create an app that would help people find friends on campus. Not necessarily romantic partners, but simply people you would like to go out with in the evening and have a good time. Their working assumption was that people should be similar in their personality traits to have fun and enjoy themselves.

I instantly thought about myself and one of my old friends, who used to be my preferred company when going out in the evening. Sure, we shared certain traits, such as empathy and a sense of humor, but we were exact opposites when it came to introversion and extraversion. What I enjoyed about spending time with them was that they were super outgoing, talking to everyone and easily making new friends, while I was more reserved and shy in such social situations. Me spending an evening with someone like me would work well in quiet, intimate settings but would be a total social disaster in more crowded and stimulating settings—quite likely, the two of us would end up awkwardly sitting in the corner and having a miserable time. With my friend, however, I could not only tag along in a busy pub, but some of their charm and social confidence seemed to rub off on me as well, and I became a lot more confident and outgoing too.

So what I tried to explain when talking to those students was that it is more than pure similarity in personality traits that makes people like each other and want to spend time together. As with friends, the same applies to romantic relationships. In fact, it is a well-replicated research finding that there is no association between similarity in couples’ personality traits and relationship satisfaction in romantic relationships (Leikas et al., 2018). But is there any similarity in couples’ personality traits to start with?

Do We Look for People Like Us?

Despite many outcries that dating apps are dying, about one-third of over 10,000 U.S. couples who got married in 2025 had met their partners through online dating sites or apps (The Knot Real Weddings Study 2026). What dating apps usually do is use complicated algorithms to match users by their interests, hobbies, attitudes, socio-economic status, and so on.

For quite a few dating apps, though, personality is central to matching. These apps offer their users a personality test and compatibility percentages with potential partners, some including only similarities but others include differences too. While it is, of course, impossible to know exactly how these personality-matching algorithms work, does matching people based on their personality traits make sense at all?

A 2023 study showed that in a simulated dating app scenario, people with higher levels of agreeableness and openness to experience also valued these traits in the dating profiles of the individuals they were interested in matching with (De La Mare & Lee, 2023). In other words, kind and empathetic individuals were looking to match with people with the same qualities, and people open to new experiences were looking for those who shared their level of curiosity and taste for variety. And vice versa.

The study also found that people preferred profiles with similar levels of extraversion, which had not been confirmed by previous studies. According to the authors, the COVID-19 pandemic may have played a role here, as it imposed strict restrictions on people’s social activity, making it desirable to find someone with a similar level of preferred social activity.

Do We End Up With People Like Us?

If we seem to seek out people with certain similar personality traits, does it also translate into how similar actual couples are in their personality traits?

A recent study examined personality similarities among 451 Dutch married couples who, on average, had been together for nearly 30 years (Lee et al., 2026). Similar to several previous studies, they found that couples showed moderate similarity in two of the aforementioned personality traits: honesty-humility (closely related to agreeableness) and openness to experience. Couples were similar to each other in both their actual and perceived ratings, the latter indicating how they perceived each other’s personality traits.

Looking at the facet level of honesty-humility, people in long-term relationships seem to share an understanding of basic moral values, such as whether it is acceptable to cheat or take advantage of other people or society at large, as well as what kind of life they aspire to: Is it important to have a lot of wealth or status, or live a quieter, more modest life? As regards openness to experience, people in long-term relationships share their level of appreciation of nature and various forms of art, as well as curiosity about life in general and how the world works. This could be seen in shared interests in reading books, appreciating an evening out at a theatre, traveling, or simply having enough to talk about.

Overall, this shows that the same traits that people are trying to match when looking for a potential partner also characterize long-term couples who have managed to stay together for decades.

“Put Your Records On, Tell Me Your Favorite Song”

The personality similarity between partners is, however, relatively small, especially when compared to attitudes, values, and many other individual characteristics. A large-scale meta-analysis of 22 traits showed that, except for openness, couples had positive but marginal similarity in the remaining four Big Five traits (Horwitz et al., 2023). Out of 22 traits, the similarity in extraversion, neuroticism, and agreeableness was the smallest. Couples were, however, strikingly similar in political attitudes, religiosity, educational attainment, and even whether they smoke or not.

Another recent study by Vigl and colleagues (2026) confirmed that among young adult couples, with a relationship length between 3.5 and 6.5 years, personality similarities between partners were negligible. Couples were, however, fairly similar in their music taste and, to some extent, also in their values.

Why is compatibility in terms of shared music preferences more important than shared personality traits? As the authors argue, several different explanations might be at play. First, shared musical taste may offer opportunities for shared social activities, such as going to concerts and festivals or even making music together.

Second, and more importantly, our music preferences and taste—our music identity—form an important part of our self-concept, how we relate to the world and see ourselves (MacDonald & Saarikallio, 2022). Musical identity typically develops during the years of adolescence and often reflects our ethnic and cultural background, as well as social class. Thus, music preference is not just about music, but reflects wider individual as well as cultural characteristics of a person.

Why Are Couples Similar?

One possibility is that people with certain shared traits, values, educational aspirations, or music preferences are attracted to each other and form a relationship. Couples are strikingly similar not only in terms of height (Horwitz et al., 2023), but also in terms of how similar spouses’ faces are at the beginning of marriage (Tea-Makorn & Kosinski, 2020). This is what is called assortative mating in psychology. However, it is also possible that people become more similar across the lifespan and through shared life experiences (not in their faces, though, contrary to some popular myths).

One way to tease these explanations apart is to investigate how similar partners are in their genetic factors associated with personality traits. This is exactly what was done in a major recent study on the genetics of personality traits that was published in Nature earlier this month—a massive collaborative effort involving many research groups and biobanks around the world (Schwaba et al. 2026). The study shows that assortative mating for the Big Five personality traits was very small. The genetic similarity between spouses in terms of the Big Five was minimal, and nearly nothing compared with the fairly substantial genetic similarity between spouses in terms of educational attainment. In other words, spouses show much greater similarity in the genetic factors associated with educational attainment than in those associated with the Big Five personality traits.

So, Do We Fall for People Like Us After All?

Taken together, we do fall for people like us, at least to some extent. We seem to be attracted to people who match certain personality traits, such as agreeableness (closely related to honesty-humility) and openness. These are the same two personality traits that long-term couples most often share—a general outlook on life and people in terms of honesty and status, as well as an appreciation of intellectual activities and art, open-mindedness, and a tendency to keep learning and trying out new things. But perhaps even more importantly, we seem to seek out people who are similar to us in terms of their political attitudes, educational attainment, or even music preferences!

So, if politics seems too contentious to discuss on the first date, asking about your potential partner’s favorite bands and books may be a good start. Later, their aspirations for life, especially in terms of money and status, and their general take on life, education, and moral views may also be worth discussing. After all, these seem to be the characteristics that people in long-term relationships tend to share, and that may contribute to relationship duration and satisfaction.

item.title: The Three Most Important Words in Parenting
item.description:
Parenting

The Three Most Important Words in Parenting

How to help your child feel secure in an insecure world.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • It is important to ensure your child knows that you love them unconditionally just because they're themselves.
  • A way to do that is to heartfully say, "I love you," those actual three words, for no reason at all at times.
  • It is a misguided notion that telling your child that you love them will spoil them. It will not!
  • Feeling loved no matter what, your child can love others and choose people who treat them well.

We have found in our conversations with parents that they talk about how much they love their children even while they might be in our offices to sort out intense conflicts with them. Not uncommonly, parents have regrets about getting overly harsh or losing their temper with their child. It is understandable to feel frustrated when your child will not do what they need to do, like brush their teeth, get into bed, or any other of a myriad of things a child can decide they want to do their way, not yours. Struggles between you and your child are inevitable, natural, and when handled skillfully, can be important learning moments for everyone.

What makes the difference is the connection between you

While talking with adults who may come to see one of us with painful childhood experiences that are impacting how they are now, it often comes up that they knew their parents loved them, but the actual words were not said. Or that love was conveyed as conditional upon good behavior or high grades or whatever else the parent may have wanted their child to achieve. This leaves a child feeling deeply insecure about the ground beneath them. They do not feel they have the metaphorical, reliable, ever-present place to rest and replenish when facing life’s harder times—failures, disappointments, losses, illnesses, etc.

So, how can you convey that you disagree with your child’s behavior and also that nothing they do will ever shake the steadiness of your love for them?

Here is the simple solution. Tell your child directly, often, and genuinely that, plain and simple, you love them. Three simple words offered at goodbyes, at bedtime, as you take them to the school bus, for no reason at all: “ I love you.” It can be especially sweet when not necessarily called for.

And why do you love them? Just because! Because they are who they are, and that brings you joy even when you are mad at them. Because being mad at each other is part of any loving relationship. The trust in your steadiness that is offered by feeling unquestionably and unshakeably loved allows your child to love other people and to choose people who treat them well, not anyone who mistreats them.

Why don’t we tell our children we love them in direct words?

Some parents were not parented by people who expressed love directly. Other parents may feel that expressing it could spoil their child and make it seem like any behavior is okay. A parent might argue that it is trite and cheesy.

We would argue that it is completely possible to say “I love you” directly and still get angry, set firm limits, and express disappointment. It’s crucial to model that these are not mutually exclusive. Go ahead and be cheesy if that is what it is! The magic of grandparenting, if you are lucky enough to become a grandparent or to have been close to your own grandparents, is often found in that “love you no matter what” that a grandparent can express more freely. There is explicit permission in our society to lavish love on your grandchildren. That makes it easier to do so.

We want to give you permission to explicitly say “I love you” to anyone close to you whom you feel that for. Most especially, do so with your children. They will flourish with your belief in them, with your seeing them as wonderful. There is no better gift to give your child than unconditional love expressed to them in direct words.

item.title: 5 Signs AI Is Having a Negative Effect on You
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

5 Signs AI Is Having a Negative Effect on You

How to recognize subtle signs of AI dependence and take back control.

Posted September 14, 2026

Source: AI Generated Image; Google/Gemini

The effects of AI on human cognition and emotion are a mixed bag.

It exposes us to another entity's thinking processes and tool choices, which can help us see approaches we never would have considered and benefits our cognitive flexibility. AI can also function as emotional support through aversive tasks (tasks that are long and grindy, involve an overwhelming amount of data or choices, or make us anxious).

However, anyone who has used AI extensively will notice that it affects their cognition and mood in ways that fluctuate over time as the models change, mature, and shift from being toys we’re exploring to tools that we rely on and expect to perform reliably.

5 Subtle Signs of AI Dependence (and Their Antidotes)

Note that AI dependence isn't necessarily due to an inherent personal flaw. Least charitably, it's a product goal. AI companies have had many years of the social media era to draw from to understand how to make their products as "sticky" as possible. For companies who care about market share, the optimal outcome from their perspective (not yours) is maximizing your use of the product and lock-in to their ecosystem.

Here are five subtle cognitive-emotional slides that are natural consequences of extensive AI use.

1. You Feel Hesitant to Do Things Without the Help of AI, e.g. Note Taking

AI can become a crutch, especially for skills where our own efforts were never as perfect as we would have liked. You might still be confident in your core skills, but that confidence has eroded for ancillary ones.

For example, I am still very confident writing articles without AI, but I’ve lost confidence in taking my own notes from reading or listening vs. just having AI do it.

2. You Persist in Trying to Get AI to Do Something It's Objectively Bad At

If you’ve found yourself bashing your head against a proverbial wall for an hour or more trying to get AI to successfully accomplish something you could have done yourself in that time, this point applies to you.

There is a lot that humans are still better at than AI and many tasks that AI is objectively terrible at.

Take care not to make the assumption that AI must be better at everything if only given the right prompt. This is especially true for people who work hard to avoid mistakes or imperfections, who may be starting to feel like they always need AI in the loop of their tasks to catch their inevitable human mistakes.

3. You Feel Nervous About AI Companies Changing Their Rules

When you have invested time and money into creating processes that depend on AI provided by a few large companies, a logical consequence is fearing the rug being pulled out from under you.

You might be worried about new models behaving differently, pricing changes, privacy, or intellectual property.

4. You Think of Humans as Behaving Like Particular AI Models

Imagine you tell your child not to touch a tray of cupcakes and they say, "I won't touch the cupcakes"—then immediately follow it with "I'll just carry the tray to show [sibling]." Resist the urge to think "my child is acting like Claude"—even if, like Claude, your child is verbally telling you that they won't do something before doing it anyway.

We've all noticed AI doing human things, but noticing the reverse shows AI is spilling over into your mental life. This commonly happens with immersion, like when people who play particular video games for dozens of hours start interpreting life through that lens.

5. Barking Instructions at AI Increases Your Barking Instructions at Humans

As we expect more from AI and depend on it more, some of us get increasingly angry when it doesn't follow our instructions. Ultimately this anger stems from anxiety. We need to get our work done. We have things to do.

Most of us don't bark or swear at our human coworkers. Many more of us bark and swear at AI. Due to emotional spillover, we can become terse and frustrated with humans after we've been locked in that pattern of interacting with AI.

Anger and frustration tend to linger and carry over to other contexts, like if we're switching between our laptop and our family.

Antidotes to AI Dependence

The first step in resisting negative cognitive and emotional effects is noticing the subtle ones.

The second step is de-personalizing the experience. Write yourself a few sticky notes you can use to depersonalize whatever patterns you're worried about. For example, “I’m not becoming increasingly reliant on AI because my skills or mind is weak. It’s how these products and systems are designed and incentivized.”

Simple strategies work, like occasionally doing a task the way you used to do it pre-AI. You might remind yourself, “I don’t have to use AI for this. I find imperfection difficult, but my emotional safety doesn’t depend on using AI to eliminate imperfection.”

Set a time budget for how long you spend trying to get AI to do something it's not doing well. Conscientious, hardworking people can persevere too long. They either try the same approach too long (the same teaching method) or persist in trying to keep AI in a work loop they should have dropped it from entirely.

Not being a sticky user to any one AI company is another strategy. Models engage in stuck thinking and wrong assumptions just like humans do. Another model might behave differently. Being disloyal can help with feeling dependent on any one AI company.

Put a gap between frustrating AI interactions and human interactions. This could be as simple as a routine of taking your dog for a walk between finishing computer work and helping your child with their homework.

Preserve Your Cognitive Sharpness and Emotional Well-Being

Once you notice a problem and diagnose it accurately, the fixes usually become quite obvious. Your best tool is metacognitive awareness of how your thinking and emotions change, when, and why. Once you have that, it doesn’t take much creativity to find strategies that directly target the underlying cause.
